end: After Prof. Yufei Ding's CSE 291P, Lecture 3
Every token listens to every token.
fine: Vaswani et al. 2017; the "too tired / too wide" pair: Google Research blog, 2017.
Threads redrawn after J. Alammar, The Illustrated Transformer (2018). The narration is a synthetic voice.
title: Attention
Who Is Listening to Whom?
en.sent0: The animal didn't cross the street
en.thrS: a trained model, redrawn after her slide 6
en.qkvS: three lists of numbers, made by three learned matrices
en.dotS: = a score: multiply number by number, add it all up
en.vToy: toy sentence: the new 'it' is about 58% 'animal'
en.hdS: each head: its own query, key and value matrices
en.bill: 1,000 tokens: 1,000,000 scores, per head, per layer

cap.n0: The animal didn't cross the street|because it was too tired. So, what is 'it'?
cap.n1: The animal, of course.|Now change one word: because it was too wide.|Now 'it' is the street.
cap.n2: Same 'it', same spot. Only the other words decide.|A language model has to work that out|with arithmetic, for every word it reads.|Lecture 3 of Prof. Yufei Ding's CSE 291P|at UC San Diego starts right here.
cap.c15: And the first is why we want to have attention.
cap.n3: Here is one trained model reading 'it'.|The sentence is cut into tokens,|words or pieces of words,|and 'it' draws a thread to every token in the sentence.|The thickest threads run to 'the animal'.
cap.c1: So attention, again, is like aggregation|of the information from other tokens.
cap.n4: Aggregation:|'it' pulls a little information out of every token.|The question is how much from each.
cap.n5: So every token is turned into three vectors,|three lists of numbers, by three learned matrices.
cap.n6: Think of a party.|The query is the question card you hold up:|what am I looking for?|The key is your name tag, what you show the others.|And the value is the parcel|you hand over when you get picked.
cap.n7: 'it' holds its question card up to every name tag.|To score a match, multiply the query and the key|number by number, and add it all up.|That's a dot product:|big when the two point the same way.
cap.n8: Then softmax turns the scores|into shares that add up to one.|With toy numbers, 'it' gives 58 percent|of its attention to 'animal', 21 to 'tired',|13 to 'street', and crumbs to the rest.
cap.n9: Her slide writes the whole recipe in one line:|every query against every key,|divided by the square root of dₖ,|softmaxed, then used to mix the values.|dₖ is how many numbers each query and key holds.|Here is her two-token example, after the softmax.
cap.c23: So that's why if you sum up each line,|you will add up to one.
cap.n10: Row one: 0.119 and 0.881.|Row two: 0.182 and 0.818.|Softmax only sees gaps:|0.881 just means the second score|was 2 higher than the first.
cap.n11: Then the mix.|Token one's new vector is 0.119 of the first value|plus 0.881 of the second,|like paint poured by a recipe.|In our toy sentence,|the new 'it' comes out mostly 'animal'.
cap.n12: Now the odd step: why divide by the square root of dₖ?|Her slide marks it self study,|so here is the short version.
cap.n13: Variance measures spread.|A dot product adds up dₖ products.|If the numbers are independent,|with mean zero and variance one, its variance is dₖ:|with 64 numbers, scores spread about 8 times wider.|Dividing by the square root of dₖ|brings the spread back to one.
cap.n14: Skip the division and watch.|Same toy scores, 8 times wider:|'animal' takes essentially everything,|and every other share rounds to zero.
cap.n15: A softmax that is all or nothing|hardly moves when nudged,|so its gradients, the nudges training runs on,|become tiny, and learning stalls.|Dividing by the square root of dₖ|is the temperature knob from our Lecture 1 episode,|set for you.
cap.n16: One honest footnote: the 2017 paper itself only says|its authors suspect this is the reason.
cap.n17: One pattern is not enough, though.|'it' needs a link to the animal it names,|and another to the word that describes it.
cap.c11: So that's why sometimes we want to use different head|to capture different relationships among the tokens.
cap.n18: So attention runs several heads:|copies of this whole recipe, side by side,|each with its own query, key and value matrices,|each free to look for something different.
cap.n19: On her slide, one head links 'it' to 'the animal',|and another links it to 'tired'.|So the new 'it' carries a bit of both.
cap.n20: Then the heads' outputs are glued back together|and mixed by one more matrix.|Call a token's numbers going in x, and coming out z.
cap.c27: If you look at the x and the z, you will find|that usually they will have the same number of elements.
cap.n21: So each token comes out the same size it went in.|And each head works with fewer numbers per token.
cap.c12: And the default we have here|is this dimension just equals|the hidden dimension of x|divided by the number of heads.
cap.n22: The 2017 base model had 512 numbers per token|and 8 heads, so 64 per head,|and all the heads together cost about the same|as one full-size head.|That 64 is the dₖ we divided by.
cap.n23: So, who is listening to whom?|'it' listens to every token and takes a share from each:|that is how the other words decide what 'it' means.|And every token does the same.|That's the power, and the bill:|a thousand tokens means a million scores,|in every head of every layer.
